_strings.@@1161debe137b: Working Families Tax Credit (New Mexico's state EITC) — New Mexico residents during any part of 2024 who file a PIT-1 and qualify for the federal Earned Income Credit (or would qualify but for the federal identification-number requirement, or but for the federal age limit if at least 18 but under 25 within the taxable year).
_strings.@@13eaa9076589: Form PIT-1 filed with Schedule PIT-B (Schedule of New Mexico Allocation and Apportionment of Income); nonresidents and part-year residents use PIT-B to allocate/apportion NM-source income. Mark residency status R (resident), N (non-resident), or P/F (part-year/first-year) on PIT-1; PIT-B is required when there is income from sources both inside and outside New Mexico.

_strings.@@2cb60dfe3564: New Mexico Child Day Care Credit — A New Mexico resident who (a) provided over half the cost of maintaining a household for one or more qualifying dependents under age 15, (b) was gainfully employed during the period claimed, (c) was not receiving TANF/New Mexico Works or similar public assistance during that period, and (d) paid unreimbursed, uncompensated child day care expenses. Use the PIT-RC Section 5 worksheet and Form PIT-CG (caregiver statement).

_strings.@@6103cf1a3836: New Mexico Child Income Tax Credit — A taxpayer who is a New Mexico resident and is not a dependent of another individual, for each qualifying child (as defined under the federal Internal Revenue Code). In effect for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2023 (Section 7-2-18.34 NMSA 1978).
_strings.@@73840e88e9ab: Low-Income Comprehensive Tax Rebate (LICTR) — Any New Mexico resident who files an individual NM income tax return, is not a dependent of another individual, was not an inmate of a public institution for more than six months, and was physically present in NM for at least six months during the tax year. May be claimed even with no taxable income.
_strings.@@76016eb1323e: Treaty conformity — NM conforms to federal treaty treatment — income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is also excluded from NM income (it flows through the federal starting point; do not add it back on the NM return). (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state can conform on treaties while DECOUPLING from the federal Code for deductions or credits; see any law-change lines below.) State note: NM's resident return (PIT-1) starts from federal adjusted gross income: "LINE 9. Federal Adjusted Gross Income — Enter the federal adjusted gross income as reported on your federal Form 1040 or 1040SR, line 11" (2024 PIT-1 instructions). Income exempt from federal tax under a US tax treaty is already excluded from federal AGI and therefore flows through to NM. NM's additions to federal AGI are enumerated exclusively on Schedule PIT-ADJ lines 1-5: (1) interest/dividends from federal tax-exempt bonds, (2) federal net operating loss carryover, (3) refunded NM Section 529 contributions, (4) charitable land-donation deduction tied to the NM land conservation credit, and (5) tax paid by a pass-through entity. None of these is an add-back of federally tax-treaty-exempt income (the word "treaty" does not appear in the 2024 PIT-ADJ instructions at all). Because there is no treaty add-back, federally treaty-exempt income is NOT re-taxed by New Mexico -> conforms. (Same analysis and result as 2023.)
_strings.@@78bf5abde4b2: 2024 PIT-1 New Mexico Personal Income Tax Return Instructions — Filing Due Date: "Paper filers: If you file by paper or pay by check your filing due date is on or before April 15, 2025. Electronic filers: If you file and pay your New Mexico Personal Income Tax return online, your due date is April 30, 2025." (The April 30 date applies only when BOTH the return and payment are electronic.)

Second pass: the Department's 2024 TAX RATE TABLE (PIT-TRT) — the mandated look-up table for PIT-1 line 18 (worked example: MFJ taxable income $25,325 -> table $834; now extended through $100,000) and its continuation schedules ('If line 17 of Form PIT-1 (Taxable Income) is over $100,000': Single $4,618 + 4.9% of excess over $100,000 to $210,000, then $10,008 + 5.9%; MFJ/HoH $4,490 + 4.9% to $315,000, then $15,025 + 5.9%; MFS $4,694 + 4.9% to $157,500, then $7,512 + 5.9%; footnote '* This column must also be used by surviving spouse'), retrieved from the Department's document library, listed on tax.newmexico.gov/forms-publications/ (no .gov copy of the file exists): https://klvg4oyd4j.execute-api.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/prod/PublicFiles/34821a9573ca43e7b06dfad20f5183fd/8c12623f-2127-489a-886f-6efb1cd55d0e/2024pit-trt.pdf — the 5.9% continuation constants (10,008/15,025/7,512) are digit-identical to 2023, confirming the schedules did not change.
_strings.@@cac2ef6513f0: Property Tax Rebate for Persons 65 or Older — New Mexico residents who were age 65 or older on the last day of the tax year, were physically present in NM at least six months, are not eligible to be claimed as a dependent, and were not a public-institution inmate more than six months. Both homeowners (property tax billed) and renters (rent paid on principal residence) may qualify.

state_tax.work_common_tail: . Tax line: 2024 Form PIT-1, line 18: 'New Mexico Tax' with line 18a Rate Table Indicator ('R = Rate tables'). 2024 PIT-1 instructions, LINE 18: 'Unless you qualify for Schedule CC, calculate your New Mexico tax by using one of these methods and then complete line 18a: If you have income from sources inside and outside New Mexico, use your entry on PIT-B, line 14 or; Use the rate tables from the PIT-1 instructions, starting on page 1T.' Applied to line 17 New Mexico Taxable Income ('Add lines 9, 10, and 11, then subtract lines 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16. If the result is negative, enter zero.'). This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: TY2024 = TY2023 schedules, LAST YEAR of the five-bracket structure: the 2024 rate schedules and bounds are identical to 2023 (Section 7-2-7 NMSA 1978 as enacted in 2019, in force since TY2021), and the 2024 omnibus tax legislation restructures Section 7-2-7 into a SIX-bracket schedule beginning tax year 2025 — the Department's 2025 PIT-TRT already prints different continuation constants (9,746/14,622/7,310 vs 2024's 10,008/15,025/7,512). Do NOT reuse this block for 2025. Base guidance: supply Form PIT-1, line 17 (New Mexico Taxable Income) = lines 9 (federal AGI) + 10 (SALT add-back for itemizers) + 11 (PIT-ADJ additions) MINUS lines 12-16, zero floor. Every deduction/exemption is computed ON THE FORM, so none ship as keys: line 12 is the filer's OWN federal standard or itemized deduction amount (whatever was allowable on federal Form 1040 line 12); line 13 is the $4,000 'Deduction for Certain Dependents' (HoH or MFJ filers only, and the worksheet multiplies $4,000 by total dependents MINUS ONE — do not model it as a flat per-dependent amount); line 14 is the New Mexico low- and middle-income tax exemption (up to $2,500 per exemption, phasing with AGI and filing status — 2024 gates: single AGI $36,667 or less, MFJ/SS or HoH $55,000 or less, MFS $27,500 or less); line 15 is PIT-ADJ deductions/exemptions; line 16 the medical care expense deduction. Do NOT supply raw federal AGI. Adjudication note (two-pass): pass 1 = the statutory Section 7-2-7 NMSA 1978 schedules (2019 HB 6, printed constants exact: $93.50/$269.50/$504.50/$10,010.50 single; $136/$392/$768/$15,027 HoH-QSS-MFJ; $68/$196/$384/$7,513.50 MFS); pass 2 = the 2024 PIT-TRT look-up table, whose rows and 5.9% continuation constants are digit-identical to the 2023 edition. One mechanical change: the 2024 table now runs through $100,000 (2023 stopped at $96,000), so the continuation schedule starts at $100,000 with chained constants $4,618/$4,490/$4,694. CRITICAL — the filed line 18 value comes from the MANDATED look-up table, which sits a few dollars BELOW statutory marginal math: for line 17 of $100,000 or less the 2024 TRT table row (in $100 bands, computed at band midpoints) is the filed figure; over $100,000 the TRT continuation schedule CHAINS FROM THE LAST TABLE ROW (single: your tax is $4,618 + 4.9% of the excess over $100,000; $4,490 MFJ/HoH; $4,694 MFS) instead of the statutory cumulative ($4,620.50 / $4,492 / $4,696), so the filed figure runs about $2-$3 below this engine's statutory bracket math at high incomes (TRT top-tier constants $10,008/$15,025/$7,512 vs statutory $10,010.50/$15,027/$7,513.50). The filed form must take the table/schedule value — never plain bracket arithmetic (the NM hand-fill pack's line 18 carries the same mandate). Statuses: the statute groups 'heads of household, surviving spouses and married individuals filing joint returns' on ONE schedule — head_of_household here is the SAME schedule as married_filing_jointly (copied per the schema, not derived), and the TRT prints identical MFJ and HoH columns with the footnote '* This column must also be used by surviving spouse', so qualifying surviving spouse maps to married_filing_jointly exactly as the engine assumes. The single schedule also applies to estates and trusts (Section 7-2-7(C) NMSA 1978: 'For single individuals and for estates and trusts'). Not modeled on the same return: line 19 additional tax on lump-sum distributions (NM's 5x averaging method, Line 19 worksheet); PIT-B allocation/apportionment for income from sources inside and outside New Mexico (line 18 then comes from PIT-B line 14, indicator B); line 20 credit for taxes paid to another state; PIT-CR business credits; and the refundable credits/rebates (Working Families Tax Credit 25% of the federal EIC, Child Income Tax Credit, PIT-RC rebates) — all tax credits or separate computations, never base reductions. New Mexico has no state-defined standard deduction or personal exemption of its own — the federal deduction flows through on line 12 (federal Form 1040 line 12 amount), which is why the caller supplies the form's own taxable-income line.
